Once the device arrives, it is connected to the on-premises network (Option A). Data is then transferred from the on-premises storage to the Snowball Edge device (Option D). Finally, the device is shipped back to AWS (Option B) for data ingestion into Amazon S3.

text: A solutions architect is tasked with transferring a large amount of data from an on-premises NFS share to Amazon S3. Order the steps for setting up and using AWS DataSync for this transfer.
options: ["Deploy the AWS DataSync agent in the on-premises environment.","Create a DataSync transfer task specifying source and destination locations.","Start the DataSync task to initiate the data transfer.","Configure source (NFS) and destination (S3) locations in DataSync."]
explanation: The first step is to deploy the AWS DataSync agent (Option A) within the on-premises environment to facilitate data transfer. Next, the source (NFS) and destination (S3) locations are configured (Option D) within DataSync. Then, a DataSync transfer task is created (Option B) to define the transfer parameters. Finally, the DataSync task is started (Option C) to begin the data transfer.

text: A development team wants to containerize a legacy application and deploy it to Amazon ECS. Order the typical steps involved in this process.
options: ["Create a Dockerfile to define the application's container image.","Push the Docker image to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR).","Build the Docker image from the Dockerfile.","Define an Amazon ECS task definition for the application."]
explanation: The process begins by creating a Dockerfile (Option A) to specify how the application should be packaged into a container. Next, the Docker image is built (Option C) using the Dockerfile. The built image is then pushed to Amazon ECR (Option B) for storage. Finally, an Amazon ECS task definition (Option D) is defined, referencing the ECR image, to describe how the container should run on ECS.

text: A solutions architect is implementing the Strangler Fig pattern to modernize a monolithic application. Order the conceptual steps for applying this pattern.
options: ["Identify a specific module or functionality to extract from the monolith.","Build the new, modernized service in AWS, independent of the monolith.","Gradually route increasing amounts of traffic from the monolith to the new service.","Decommission the corresponding functionality within the original monolithic application."]
explanation: The Strangler Fig pattern starts by identifying a specific module (Option A) within the monolith that can be independently extracted. Next, the new, modernized service is built (Option B) in AWS. Traffic is then gradually routed (Option C) from the old module to the new service. Once the new service is fully operational and handling all traffic, the old functionality in the monolith is decommissioned (Option D).

text: Order the steps to deploy a new service to an Amazon ECS cluster.
options: ["Configure service details (desired count, load balancing)","Select the ECS cluster and launch type","Choose a task definition","Review and create the service"]
explanation: To deploy a new service to an Amazon ECS cluster, you first select the ECS cluster and launch type (Option B) where the service will run. Next, choose an existing task definition (Option C) that defines your application's containers. Then, configure service details (Option A), such as the desired number of tasks and load balancer integration. Finally, review the configuration and create the service (Option D).

text: A development team has a Docker image ready for deployment. Order the steps to run it as a service on Amazon ECS with Fargate.
options: ["Create an Amazon ECS cluster with Fargate launch type","Define an Amazon ECS task definition referencing the image","Push the Docker image to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR)","Create an Amazon ECS service using the task definition"]
explanation: First, push the Docker image to Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR) (Option C) to make it accessible to ECS. Next, create an Amazon ECS cluster with Fargate launch type (Option A) if one doesn't already exist. Then, define an Amazon ECS task definition (Option B) that references the ECR image and specifies Fargate compatibility. Finally, create an Amazon ECS service (Option D) using this task definition to run and maintain the desired number of tasks.

text: Order the steps to update an existing Amazon ECS service with a new task definition.
options: ["Create a new revision of the task definition with updated container image or settings","Monitor the service deployment and health checks","Update the existing Amazon ECS service to use the new task definition revision","Ensure the new Docker image is available in Amazon ECR"]
explanation: Before updating, ensure the new Docker image is available in Amazon ECR (Option D) if the update involves a new image. Next, create a new revision of the task definition (Option A) incorporating the updated container image or settings. Then, update the existing Amazon ECS service (Option C) to point to this new task definition revision. Finally, monitor the service deployment and health checks (Option B) to ensure a successful rollout.

options: ["Identify bounded contexts within the monolith suitable for extraction.","Extract and deploy individual services independently.","Refactor communication patterns between services to be asynchronous and resilient.","Gradually replace monolithic components with new microservices."]
explanation: The modernization process begins by identifying bounded contexts (Option A) within the monolith that can become independent services. Next, monolithic components are gradually replaced (Option D) with new microservices, often using patterns like the Strangler Fig. As services are extracted, they are deployed independently (Option B). Finally, communication patterns (Option C) between these new services are refactored to be more cloud-native, asynchronous, and resilient.

text: A solutions architect needs to host a static website on AWS in a cost-effective and highly available manner. Order the steps for setting up a static website using Amazon S3.
options: ["Create an Amazon S3 bucket.","Upload all static website files (HTML, CSS, JS, images) to the S3 bucket.","Enable static website hosting for the S3 bucket.","Configure a bucket policy to allow public read access to the website content."]
explanation: The first step is to create an Amazon S3 bucket (Option A) which will store the website content. Next, all static website files (Option B) are uploaded to this bucket. Then, static website hosting (Option C) is enabled for the bucket. Finally, a bucket policy (Option D) is configured to grant public read access, making the website accessible.
